categories.name: Foundry platform
categories.description: Projects, hubs, model deployment, agents, guardrails, and access control in Microsoft Foundry.

features.name: Create a Foundry project
features.summary: Create a Foundry project in the new Foundry portal, which also creates the Foundry resource it lives on.
features.whyItMatters: A project is the container for agents, evaluations, and files, and every later lab in the new portal starts from one. Knowing that a Foundry project sits on a Foundry resource separates it from a hub-based project.
concepts: A Foundry project is a child of a Foundry resource. The portal creates the resource automatically when you create the first project, and extra projects can share the same resource.
Projects can have their own access controls but share settings such as network security, deployments, and tool integration from the parent resource.
This procedure is for Foundry projects only. Hub-based projects use a hub and are created differently; see the hub-based project feature in this file.
steps: Confirm you have an Azure subscription and a role that can create a Foundry resource, such as **Foundry Account Owner** or **Foundry Owner**.
Sign in to Microsoft Foundry at https://ai.azure.com and make sure the **New Foundry** toggle is on.
Select the project name in the upper-left corner, then select **Create new project**.
Enter a project name and select **Create project**.
For more control, open **Advanced options**, choose a **Resource group** and **Location**, then select **Create**.
When provisioning finishes, open the project **Home** page and note the project endpoint.
To add another project to the same resource, select **Manage**, then **Resource details**, then **Add project**.
validation: The project overview page appears and the project name shows in the upper-left corner.
The project **Home** page shows a project endpoint in the form https://<resource-name>.services.ai.azure.com/api/projects/<project-name>.
learnQueries: Create a project for Microsoft Foundry

features.name: Deploy a model and test it in the playground
features.summary: Deploy a model from the Model Catalog into a Foundry project and try it in the playground.
features.whyItMatters: A deployment is what applications and agents call, so deploying and testing a model is the first checkpoint for any build. The playground lets you confirm behavior before writing code.
concepts: This procedure is for Foundry projects in the new portal. You need a paid Azure subscription, the Cognitive Services Contributor role or equivalent on the Foundry resource, and a Foundry project.
Models from partners and community require an Azure Marketplace subscription and the permissions to create one; Foundry Models sold by Azure do not.

For hub-based projects use the Foundry (classic) portal. The classic chat playground quickstart says it works with either project type and uses the model catalog, **Use this model**, and **Open in playground**. Full hub-based deployment options: Not confirmed in Microsoft Learn.
steps: Sign in to Microsoft Foundry at https://ai.azure.com and make sure the **New Foundry** toggle is on.
Open your Foundry project, then go to **Build** > **Catalog** > **Model Catalog**.
Select a model and review its model card.
Select **Deploy** > **Default settings**, or **Deploy** > **Custom settings** to change deployment settings.
For a partner or community model, read the terms and select **Agree and Proceed** to subscribe through Azure Marketplace.
Keep or edit the deployment name, then select **Deploy**.
When deployment completes you land in the playground; type a prompt and review the output.
Select the **Code** tab to see how to call the deployment from code.
validation: The deployment status shows **Succeeded** in your deployment list (**Build** > **Models**).
A prompt sent in the playground returns a model response.
learnQueries: Deploy Microsoft Foundry Models in the Foundry portal

features.name: Create a hub and a hub-based project
features.summary: Create a Foundry hub in the Azure portal, then create a hub-based project from it in the Foundry (classic) portal.
features.whyItMatters: Hub-based projects remain the option for prompt flow, managed compute, and Azure Machine Learning compatibility. Hubs let an admin set security, connections, and spend once for many projects.
concepts: A hub is an Azure Machine Learning-based resource that groups projects and shares security, connections, compute and quota, and policy with them. Creating a hub also provisions a Foundry resource.

Learn says to prefer a Foundry project in most cases, and that new agents and model-centric capabilities are only available on Foundry projects. Agents are listed as preview only on hub-based projects.
This procedure applies only to hub-based projects in the Foundry (classic) portal. It does not work for Foundry projects.
steps: Confirm you have an Azure subscription and the Contributor or Owner role on the resource group; project creation needs Owner or Contributor on the hub resource.
In the Azure portal, search for `Foundry`, select **AI Hubs**, then select **+ Create** and **Hub**.
Enter the hub name, subscription, resource group, and location. For **Azure AI services base models**, select an existing Foundry resource or create a new one.
Set the **Storage**, **Inbound Access**, **Outbound Access**, **Encryption**, and **Identity** tabs as needed, then select **Review + create** > **Create**.
Sign in to Microsoft Foundry at https://ai.azure.com and turn the **New Foundry** toggle off to use Foundry (classic).
Select **Create new** (or the project breadcrumb, then **Create new resource**), choose **AI hub resource**, and select **Next**.
Enter a project name, choose your hub in the dropdown (or **Create a new hub**), and select **Create**.
Open the project **Overview** page to see its name, subscription, and resource group.
validation: The project breadcrumb shows **(Hub)** on its second line, which identifies a hub-based project.
The project appears under the hub, and the **Overview** page shows the project name, subscription, and resource group.

features.name: Create a prompt agent with Foundry Agent Service
features.summary: Create a declarative prompt agent from a deployed model and instructions, then chat with it across two turns.
features.whyItMatters: A prompt agent is the lowest-effort agent in Foundry Agent Service: Foundry hosts it and you supply only a model, instructions, and optional tools. It is the starting point before moving to hosted agents.
concepts: A prompt agent is declaratively defined: it combines a model from the model catalog, instructions, tools, and prompts. The quickstart uses Azure AI Projects 2.x, which is incompatible with 1.x.

This procedure is for Foundry projects. Learn lists agents as GA on Foundry projects and preview only on hub-based projects. The quickstart's portal tab has no portal creation steps; portal-based agent creation: Not confirmed in Microsoft Learn.
The quickstart expects a deployed model and Application Insights connected to the project with permission to read traces.
steps: Make sure you have a Foundry project, a deployed model (for example gpt-5-mini), and Application Insights connected to the project.
Run `pip install "azure-ai-projects>=2.3.0"` and sign in with `az login`.
Copy the project endpoint from the project welcome screen; it has the form https://<resource-name>.services.ai.azure.com/api/projects/<project-name>.
In your script, set the project endpoint and an agent name, and create an `AIProjectClient` with `DefaultAzureCredential`.
Call `project.agents.create_version` with a `PromptAgentDefinition` that sets the model and the instructions.
Get an agent-bound client with `project.get_openai_client(agent_name=...)` and create a conversation.
Call `openai.responses.create` with the conversation ID and a question, then send a related follow-up in the same conversation.
When finished, delete the resource group in the Azure portal if you no longer need the resources.
validation: The console prints the agent ID, name, and version after creation.
The follow-up answer reflects the earlier question, showing the agent keeps conversation history.

features.name: Configure guardrails for models and agents
features.summary: Create a guardrail with risk controls, assign it to models and agents, and test it in the playground.
features.whyItMatters: Guardrails set what content is detected and blocked at each intervention point, and changes take effect on live deployments. Testing them on a non-production model avoids surprises.
concepts: In the new portal a guardrail is a set of controls (a risk, intervention points, and an action) assigned to models and agents. In the REST API a guardrail is a RAI policy on the resource, assigned through the deployment's `raiPolicyName`.
You need a Foundry project, at least one model deployment, and the Foundry Account Owner role or higher. Microsoft Default guardrails such as Default.V2 can't be edited.

For hub-based projects and the classic portal, content filters are created under **Guardrails + controls** > **Content filters** and applied from **Models + endpoints** > **Edit**. That is a different procedure from the one below.
steps: Open your project in https://ai.azure.com, select **Build**, then the **Guardrails** page, and select **Create Guardrail**.
In Step 1: Add Controls, select a risk from the dropdown.
Choose intervention points and one action, then select **Add control**.
Select **Next** for Step 2, then use **Add agents** and **Add models** to pick what the guardrail applies to, and select **Save**.
Select **Next** for Step 3: Review, name the guardrail, and select **Create**.
Select the guardrail row, then select **Try in Playground**; if the button is missing, assign the guardrail to a model or agent first.
Send test queries and look for the chat message that names the detected risk and intervention point when a control with the action "Annotate and block" triggers.
validation: The new guardrail appears in the list on the **Guardrails** page and shows the models and agents it applies to.
A test prompt that triggers an "Annotate and block" control shows a message with the risk and intervention point.

features.name: Grant access with Foundry roles
features.summary: Assign Foundry built-in roles at the right scope so builders, managers, and agent consumers get least-privilege access.
features.whyItMatters: Foundry separates managing accounts, creating projects, building, and calling agents into different roles. Correct scoping lets a team build without broad subscription rights.
concepts: RBAC applies when you authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID; key-based authentication grants full access without role restrictions. Scopes are subscription, resource group, Foundry resource, Foundry project, and individual agent.

Key roles are Foundry Agent Consumer, Foundry User, Foundry Project Manager, Foundry Account Owner, and Foundry Owner. Do not use Azure AI Developer for Foundry projects; it is scoped to Azure Machine Learning workspaces and hubs.
This is for Foundry projects. Hub-based projects use a separate hub-focused RBAC article with roles such as Azure AI Developer and Reader at the hub and project levels.
steps: Choose the role and scope per persona, for example Foundry User on the project for developers and Foundry Agent Consumer for callers that only use agent endpoints.
In the Azure portal, open your Foundry resource and go to **Access control (IAM)**.
Create a role assignment for **Foundry User**, set **Members** to **User, group, or service principal**, select the principal, and select **Review + assign**.
Repeat with **Members** set to **Managed identity** and select your project's managed identity.
Alternatively in the Foundry portal, select **Manage** > **Project details**, open the **Users** tab, select **Add user**, enter the email address, and select **Add**.
If users need quota visibility, assign **Cognitive Services Usages Reader** at the subscription scope.
Use role definition IDs instead of names in scripts because of the role rename; Foundry User is 53ca6127-db72-4b80-b1b0-d745d6d5456d.
validation: The role assignment appears under **Access control (IAM)** for the Foundry resource or project, for example in the output of `az role assignment list --scope <project-id>`.
A team member signs in to https://ai.azure.com, can select the project, and sees deployed models under **Build** > **Models**.
